newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to aim for fewer deficit-financing bonds-MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan to aim for fewer deficit-financing bonds-MOF.

text.p: Japan's Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said on Tuesday that his ministry is currently working towards issuing fewer deficit-financing bonds for the fiscal year starting in April 1997 than it will in 1996/97.

Asked about the Tokyo Nikkei stock average's fall to below 20,000 this morning, Kubo told a news conference: "Although the market is the focus of attention because it (the Nikkei) is moving around the key 20,000 level, the fluctuation is not so big. I think the drop was partly affected by movements in the New York market."
In Tuesday's morning trade, the Nikkei index slipped below 20,000 for the first time since March 15, although it had recovered to 20,195.84 by the midday close.
"September has just started, so I would like more detailed reports on future stock movements and the factors moving the markets now, and pass my own judgement," Kubo said.
Japanese companies use the stock price level at the end of September to settle book losses or profits in stock investments for the April to September period.

On deficit-financing bonds, Kubo admitted that it would be impossible to abolish such issues next fiscal year after looking at the 1997/98 budget requests submitted by various ministries at the end of August.
Unless budget reforms are carried out, it is "highly possible" that MOF may be forced to issue more than 12 trillion yen worth of deficit-financing bonds this fiscal year, Kubo said.
"We would be able to back up our claim that next year would be the beginning of fiscal reforms, if we can issue fewer deficit-financing bonds than in 1996/97," he said.
The ministry would keep in mind such a goal when assessing the budgetary requests to come up with the final MOF draft at the end of December, he said.

On the supplementary budget, Kubo said he met with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Sunday and the two agreed to look at overall economic conditions in the first half of calendar 1996 before making a final decision.

He added that it would be difficult to say now whether the government would view the economic recovery as being on track even if the April-June gross national product figures, to be released around mid-September, show a negative growth.
Kubo also reminded Hashimoto that MOF needed "a considerable number of days" to come up with an extra budget and the two agreed to keep close contact as needed.

Kubo said he also told Hashimoto that the government would need about 10 trillion yen of extra funds if it was to carry out a large extra budget featuring economic stimulus steps and continued tax breaks as advocated by some politicians.
Continuing special income tax cuts would cut revenues by two trillion yen and a freezing of the consumption tax hike would mean about five trillion yen less in revenues, he said.
"A large supplementary budget would entail at least three trillion yen worth of government spending," Kubo added.

Cabinet ministers have decided to increase the consumption tax to five percent from the current three percent from next April, but have been met with opposition from politicians ahead of expected general elections.
